entity: workers' compensation insurers, employers and risk managers, especially in transportation, warehousing and delivery
business_impact: An insurance industry study of 22 years of workers' compensation claims in 35 states found that claims rise much more on cold, wet days than on cold, dry days: on wet days with highs between 25 and 40°F there were 7 to 10 percent more injury claims than on mild, dry days, against 1 to 3 percent on dry days at the same temperatures, mainly from slips and falls and secondarily from vehicle crashes. Transportation and warehousing saw the largest cold-day effects.
story_seed: A cold, wet day with rain, snow or a wintry mix is forecast for {metro} — a Weather Company meteorologist on timing, temperatures and how long surfaces stay slick, for employers and workers' comp insurers thinking about slips, falls and work-vehicle crashes

evidence.source: Coate, Scott and Colón, "Adverse Weather and Workers Compensation Claims," NCCI research brief, October 2024 (pp. 7, 9-10; Tables 2-3)

entity: workers' compensation insurers, employers and risk managers, especially in construction, landscaping and other outdoor work
business_impact: An insurance industry study of 22 years of workers' compensation claims in 35 states found injury claims rise steadily with the day's high temperature, with the largest increases on hot days in outdoor sectors such as construction, natural resources and landscaping. It also estimated that a summer with more hot days than a city is used to would raise claims by a similar amount in warmer and cooler cities.

evidence.source: Coate, Scott and Colón, "Adverse Weather and Workers Compensation Claims," NCCI research brief, October 2024 (pp. 7-8, 13, 16; Table 1)

entity: homeowners, renters and flood insurance buyers
business_impact: Federal flood insurance guidance says standard homeowners policies do not, as a rule, cover flooding, and that many homeowners don't realize it until it is too late. Flood coverage can be bought at any time, but there is generally a 30-day waiting period after applying and paying before the policy takes effect.

entity: owners and managers of buildings with flat and low-slope roofs, homeowners, and property insurers
business_impact: Federal snow-load guidance for building owners says a foot of fresh snow can weigh from about 3 pounds per square foot when light and dry to 21 when wet and heavy, that rain on snow can add to the load, and that when snow already on a roof is near its capacity and more snow is forecast, removal by a licensed, insured roofing contractor is prudent. It also warns that snow on the ground is not a measure of the load on a roof.

entity: homeowners and renters in storm country, and consumer reporters
business_impact: State insurance regulators warn that home repair fraud is common after storms that damage many homes, with contractors coming into hard-hit areas to take advantage of storm victims. Their guidance says no one is required to sign an assignment of benefits, which lets a roofer or other contractor deal with the insurer and collect payment directly, to get repairs done; it advises using local or trusted companies, getting more than one bid, photographing damage first and contacting the insurer as soon as possible.
